To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) black-box adversaries can craft adversarial examples for DNNs with a success rate of 84.24%, (2) this attack can be performed with no knowledge of the DNN model or its training data, and (3) this attack can evade previously proposed defenses.
(1) we demonstrate the first black-box attack against remote DNNs, and (2) we show that this attack is capable of evasive evasion, that is, of evading defenses designed to make it harder.
we have developed a black-box attack strategy that is practical and can be applied against DNNs and other models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how can a black-box attacker control a remotely hosted ML model?
the practicality of adversarial example attacks against ML, and we demonstrate that they can be performed against remote DNNs with no knowledge of their internals or training data.
the security of ML systems and their ability to withstand adversarial inputs, and we find that the state of the art in ML security is far from adequate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our work is the first practical demonstration that adversarial examples are a real threat against remotely hosted ML models, even if they are trained using state-of-the-art defenses.
the current state of machine learning models and their defenses are not secure against adversarial examples.

our work demonstrates a practical black-box attack strategy against machine learning models, with a success rate of 84.24%, 96.19%, and 88.9%, on three models from three different companies, without any knowledge of the models or their training data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the current state-of-the-art in adversarial example crafting can be used to attack remotely-hosted ML models without knowledge of either model internals or its data, and with no access to the training data.
we demonstrate that it is possible to attack remotely hosted DNNs with no knowledge of either the DNN internals or its training set.
the adversarial examples we crafted were misclassified by the remote DNNs at rates of 84.24%, 96.19%, and 88.93%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ML models are vulnerable to adversarially modified inputs even in the black-box setting.
the security of DNNs and ML in general is not improved by black-boxing them, as they are still vulnerable to attacks that do not require access to the model internals or training data.
ML models, even those hosted remotely by third parties and not exposed to the attacker, may be vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
